claim: The study used a 6 x 6 x 5 μm³ complete 3DEM reconstruction from the middle of stratum radiatum in hippocampal area CA1.
source: In a 6 x 6 x 5 μm3 complete 3DEM from the middle of stratum radiatum in hippocampal area CA1 (Mishchenko et al., 2010; Kinney et al., 2013; see Materials and Methods).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the dimensions and location of the 3DEM reconstruction with supporting citations.

claim: 449 synapses were identified in the reconstructed volume.
source: We identified 449 synapses, 446 axons and 149 dendrites, which except for one identified branch point, are likely to originate from different neurons based on the size of the reconstructed volume and the obtuse branching angles of dendrites from these neurons (Ishizuka et al., 1995; Megı́as et al., 1997).
evidence: Direct statement of the number of synapses identified in the reconstruction.

claim: 446 axons were identified in the reconstructed volume.
source: We identified 449 synapses, 446 axons and 149 dendrites, which except for one identified branch point, are likely to originate from different neurons based on the size of the reconstructed volume and the obtuse branching angles of dendrites from these neurons (Ishizuka et al., 1995; Megı́as et al., 1997).
evidence: Direct statement of the number of axons identified in the reconstruction.

claim: 149 dendrites were identified in the reconstructed volume.
source: We identified 449 synapses, 446 axons and 149 dendrites, which except for one identified branch point, are likely to originate from different neurons based on the size of the reconstructed volume and the obtuse branching angles of dendrites from these neurons (Ishizuka et al., 1995; Megı́as et al., 1997).
evidence: Direct statement of the number of dendrites identified in the reconstruction.

claim: The dendrites, except for one identified branch point, are likely to originate from different neurons based on the size of the reconstructed volume and the obtuse branching angles.
source: We identified 449 synapses, 446 axons and 149 dendrites, which except for one identified branch point, are likely to originate from different neurons based on the size of the reconstructed volume and the obtuse branching angles of dendrites from these neurons (Ishizuka et al., 1995; Megı́as et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the volume size and branching angles, with citations to prior work.

claim: The correlation between spine head area and spine head volume accounted for 99% of the variance.
source: The correlation between spine head area and spine head volume accounted for 99% of the variance, despite the wide range in spine head shapes and dimensions (Figure 1A), which suggests that the accuracy of our measurements matched the precision of the spine.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1A showing the correlation.

claim: There is a weak trend between neck diameter and spine head volume.
source: We also measured spine neck length, diameter, and volume and found a weak trend between the neck diameter (Figure 1D) and spine head volume but no correlation between neck length (Figure 1E) and spine head volume, consistent with previous studies (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Tønnesen et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1D and citations to previous studies.

claim: There is no correlation between neck length and spine head volume.
source: We also measured spine neck length, diameter, and volume and found a weak trend between the neck diameter (Figure 1D) and spine head volume but no correlation between neck length (Figure 1E) and spine head volume, consistent with previous studies (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Tønnesen et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1E and citations to previous studies.

claim: Spine head volumes ranged in size over a factor of 60 from smallest to largest.
source: We found that spine head volumes ranged in size over a factor of 60 from smallest to largest while the CV of any given size was 0.083 and was constant across the range of sizes.
evidence: Direct statement of the range of spine head volumes observed.

claim: The coefficient of variation (CV) of spine head volume was 0.083 and was constant across the range of sizes.
source: We found that spine head volumes ranged in size over a factor of 60 from smallest to largest while the CV of any given size was 0.083 and was constant across the range of sizes.
evidence: Direct statement of the CV value and its constancy.

claim: Approximately 26 different mean synaptic strengths can span the entire range of spine sizes.
source: Using this logic, we found that ~26 different mean synaptic strengths could span the entire range, assuming CV = 0.083 for each strength level, and a 69% discrimination threshold (Figure 8, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Direct statement based on signal detection theory calculations with reference to Figure 8.

claim: Each synapse can store 4.7 bits of information as synaptic strength.
source: These 26 distinct strength levels can be represented with 4.7 bits of information (i.e. 24.7 ≈ 26) which means 4.7 bits of information that can be stored at each synapse as synaptic strength.
evidence: Direct calculation from the number of distinguishable strength levels.

claim: Pairs of spines on the same dendrite that received input from the same axon ('axon-coupled') were of the same size and had nearly identical head volumes.
source: Pairs of spines on the same dendrite that received input from the same axon ('axon-coupled'), were of the same size and had nearly identical head volumes (Figure 4).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4 showing the data.

claim: The paired head volumes of axon-coupled spines on the same dendrite were highly correlated with slope 0.91.
source: When plotted against one another, the paired head volumes were highly correlated with slope 0.91, and despite the small sample size, were highly significantly different from random pairings of spines (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, KS test p=0.0002).
evidence: Direct statement with statistical analysis and reference to figures.

claim: The paired head volumes of axon-coupled spines on the same dendrite were highly significantly different from random pairings (KS test p=0.0002).
source: When plotted against one another, the paired head volumes were highly correlated with slope 0.91, and despite the small sample size, were highly significantly different from random pairings of spines (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, KS test p=0.0002).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result.

claim: There was a strong positive correlation between paired neck diameters of axon-coupled spines on the same dendrite.
source: Similarly, there was a strong positive correlation between their paired neck diameters (Figure 4D), PSD areas (Figure 4E), and number of presynaptic docked vesicles (Figure 4F).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: There was a strong positive correlation between paired PSD areas of axon-coupled spines on the same dendrite.
source: Similarly, there was a strong positive correlation between their paired neck diameters (Figure 4D), PSD areas (Figure 4E), and number of presynaptic docked vesicles (Figure 4F).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: There was a strong positive correlation between the number of presynaptic docked vesicles of axon-coupled spines on the same dendrite.
source: Similarly, there was a strong positive correlation between their paired neck diameters (Figure 4D), PSD areas (Figure 4E), and number of presynaptic docked vesicles (Figure 4F).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: The spine neck lengths of axon-coupled pairs on the same dendrite were not well-correlated.
source: In contrast, the spine neck lengths (Figure 4G), and neck volumes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) of the pairs were not well-correlated indicating that regulation of neck length and neck volume are not important for synaptic strength.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4G.

claim: The spine neck volumes of axon-coupled pairs on the same dendrite were not well-correlated.
source: In contrast, the spine neck lengths (Figure 4G), and neck volumes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) of the pairs were not well-correlated indicating that regulation of neck length and neck volume are not important for synaptic strength.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Regulation of neck length and neck volume are not important for synaptic strength.
source: In contrast, the spine neck lengths (Figure 4G), and neck volumes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) of the pairs were not well-correlated indicating that regulation of neck length and neck volume are not important for synaptic strength.
evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of correlation in neck measurements.

claim: The median value of the coefficient of variation of volume differences between axon-coupled pairs on the same dendrite was CV = 0.083.
source: Excluding this triple synapse, the median value of the coefficient of variation of volume differences between pairs was CV = 0.083 and was as precise for small synapses as it was for large ones (Figure 5).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5.

claim: The precision of spine size matching was as precise for small synapses as it was for large ones.
source: Excluding this triple synapse, the median value of the coefficient of variation of volume differences between pairs was CV = 0.083 and was as precise for small synapses as it was for large ones (Figure 5).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 5 showing no correlation between CV and size.

claim: The near-identical size relationship does not hold for axon-coupled spines on different dendrites (CV = 0.39, n = 127).
source: This near-identical size relationship does not hold for axon-coupled spines on different dendrites (Figure 6B, CV = 0.39, n = 127, example Figure 6A), nor for non-axon-coupled spines on the same or different dendrites (Figures 6E,F, example Figure 6D) -- all cases which would have had different activation histories.
evidence: Direct statement with data and reference to figures.

claim: The near-identical size relationship does not hold for non-axon-coupled spines on the same or different dendrites.
source: This near-identical size relationship does not hold for axon-coupled spines on different dendrites (Figure 6B, CV = 0.39, n = 127, example Figure 6A), nor for non-axon-coupled spines on the same or different dendrites (Figures 6E,F, example Figure 6D) -- all cases which would have had different activation histories.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figures.

claim: The volumes of axon-coupled different-dendrite spines are no different from the volumes of random pairs (KS test p=0.94).
source: The volumes of axon-coupled different-dendrite spines are no different from the volumes of random pairs when plotted against one another (KS test p=0.94, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, and Figures 6B,C) and the distribution of their sizes was no different from the whole population (KS test p=0.41).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result with reference to figures.

claim: The distribution of sizes of axon-coupled different-dendrite spines was no different from the whole population (KS test p=0.41).
source: The volumes of axon-coupled different-dendrite spines are no different from the volumes of random pairs when plotted against one another (KS test p=0.94, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, and Figures 6B,C) and the distribution of their sizes was no different from the whole population (KS test p=0.41).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical test result.

claim: A total of 31,377 presynaptic vesicles were identified in the reconstruction.
source: Synaptic vesicles in the presynaptic terminals, totaling 31,377 in number, were identified along with their 3D locations within the dense reconstruction.
evidence: Direct statement of the total number of vesicles identified.

claim: 3,437 vesicles were labeled as docked according to the criterion of being within 100 nm of the presynaptic membrane.
source: Of the 31,377 vesicles, 3437 were labeled as docked according to this criterion which yielded estimates in good agreement with previous estimates (Harris and Sultan, 1995; Schikorski and Stevens, 1997; Figures 2B–D).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to previous work and reference to figures.

claim: The relationship between PSD area and spine head volume did not differ significantly across different dendrites.
source: We determined that the relationship between PSD area and spine head volume did not differ significantly across different dendrites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: There is a strong correlation between size and efficacy of a synapse.
source: The strong correlation between size and efficacy of a synapse allowed us to estimate the variability of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract.

claim: Anatomical measurements of spine size, PSD area, number of AMPA receptors, area of presynaptic active zone, and number of docked vesicles are all highly correlated with each other.
source: Anatomical measurements of the spine size, the area of the postsynaptic density (PSD), the number of AMPA receptors, the area of the presynaptic active zone and the number of docked vesicles in the presynaptic terminal are all highly correlated with each other and with physiological measurements of the release probability and the efficacy of the synapse (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Lisman and Harris, 1994; Harris and Sultan, 1995; Schikorski and Stevens, 1997; Murthy et al., 2001; Branco et al., 2008; Bourne et al., 2013).
evidence: Direct statement with multiple citations to supporting literature.

claim: Anatomical measurements are highly correlated with physiological measurements of release probability and synapse efficacy.
source: Anatomical measurements of the spine size, the area of the postsynaptic density (PSD), the number of AMPA receptors, the area of the presynaptic active zone and the number of docked vesicles in the presynaptic terminal are all highly correlated with each other and with physiological measurements of the release probability and the efficacy of the synapse (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Lisman and Harris, 1994; Harris and Sultan, 1995; Schikorski and Stevens, 1997; Murthy et al., 2001; Branco et al., 2008; Bourne et al., 2013).
evidence: Direct statement with multiple citations to supporting literature.

claim: The sizes and strengths of synapses can increase or decrease according to the history of relative timing of presynaptic inputs and postsynaptic spikes.
source: The sizes and strengths of these synapses can increase or decrease according to the history of relative timing of presynaptic inputs and postsynaptic spikes (Bi and Poo, 1998).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to supporting work.

claim: Prior work suggests that pairs of spines on the same dendrite contacting the same axon are more similar in size than those from the same axon on different dendrites.
source: Prior work suggests that such pairs of spines are more similar in size than those from the same axon on different dendrites (Sorra and Harris, 1993).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to prior work.

claim: The study used three separate 3DEM data sets from three adult male rats (55–65 days old).
source: Three separate 3DEM data sets were used in this study. Each of these data sets has been used for other purposes in prior studies. Images were obtained from serial thin sections in the middle of stratum radiatum of hippocampal area CA1 from three adult male rats (55–65 days old) (Mishchenko et al., 2010; Bourne et al., 2013).
evidence: Direct statement in Materials and methods with citations.

claim: 13 axon-coupled synaptic pairs were identified on 11 dendrites in the dense model.
source: In this data set, we identified 13 axon-coupled synaptic pairs on 11 dendrites (Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: 7 axon-coupled synaptic pairs were identified on 4 dendrites in the other two data sets.
source: In this data set, we identified 7 axon-coupled synaptic pairs on 4 dendrites for a total of 20 axon-coupled dendrite-coupled spine pairs.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of pairs identified.

claim: A total of 20 axon-coupled dendrite-coupled spine pairs were analyzed across all data sets.
source: In this data set, we identified 7 axon-coupled synaptic pairs on 4 dendrites for a total of 20 axon-coupled dendrite-coupled spine pairs.
evidence: Direct statement of the total number of pairs.

claim: 287 valid synapses on dendritic spines were included in the analysis after exclusions.
source: We excluded a number of synapses from the analysis if they were partially clipped by the edge of the data set (142), or were shaft synapses (20) leaving 287 valid synapses on dendritic spines in the dense model.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of valid synapses after exclusions.

claim: 142 synapses were excluded because they were partially clipped by the edge of the data set.
source: We excluded a number of synapses from the analysis if they were partially clipped by the edge of the data set (142), or were shaft synapses (20) leaving 287 valid synapses on dendritic spines in the dense model.
evidence: Direct statement of the number and reason for exclusion.

claim: 20 shaft synapses were excluded from the analysis.
source: We excluded a number of synapses from the analysis if they were partially clipped by the edge of the data set (142), or were shaft synapses (20) leaving 287 valid synapses on dendritic spines in the dense model.
evidence: Direct statement of the number and reason for exclusion.

claim: 70 spines were excluded from the analysis of axon-coupled spines because the axon did not contact any other spines within the reconstructed volume.
source: An additional 70 spines were excluded from the analysis of axon-coupled spines as the axon which contacted these spines did not contact any other spines within the reconstructed volume.
evidence: Direct statement of the number and reason for exclusion.

claim: The standard error of the mean in spine head volume decreases with volume and is less than 5% for the majority of spines with a median error of about 1%.
source: The standard error of the mean in spine head volume decreases with volume and is less than 5% for the majority of spines with a median error of about 1% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: 236 valid presynaptic terminals were included in the analysis after exclusions.
source: Of the 449 presynaptic terminals, we excluded 193 terminals from the analysis due to truncation at the edge of the volume, and 20 terminals at shaft synapses, leaving 236 valid terminals.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of valid terminals after exclusions.

claim: 193 presynaptic terminals were excluded due to truncation at the edge of the volume.
source: Of the 449 presynaptic terminals, we excluded 193 terminals from the analysis due to truncation at the edge of the volume, and 20 terminals at shaft synapses, leaving 236 valid terminals.
evidence: Direct statement of the number and reason for exclusion.

claim: Docked vesicles were estimated by counting vesicles whose centers were located within 100 nm of the presynaptic membrane across from the postsynaptic density.
source: To estimate docked vesicles, we counted the number of vesicles whose centers were located within 100 nm of the presynaptic membrane across from the postsynaptic density of a given spine.
evidence: Direct statement of the method used to estimate docked vesicles.

claim: All regression analysis was performed using Pearson's linear regression on log-normal transformed data.
source: Consequently, all regression analysis was performed using Pearson's linear regression on the data after applying a log-normal transformation (r2 values shown in Figures 1–6).
evidence: Direct statement of the statistical method used.

claim: The coefficient of variation of the population of spine pairings was calculated as the median value of the CVs of each individual pair.
source: The coefficient of variation (CV) of the population of spine pairings (Figures 4 and 6) was calculated as the median value of the CVs of each individual pair.
evidence: Direct statement of the calculation method.

claim: The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnoff (KS) test was used to compare distributions.
source: We used the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnoff (KS) test to make these comparisons in Figures 4 and 6.
evidence: Direct statement of the statistical test used.

claim: At a discrimination threshold of 76% (corresponding to SNR = 2) there would be approximately 23 distinct strengths and 4.5 bits of information.
source: At a discrimination threshold of 76% (corresponding to SNR = 2) there would be ~23 distinct strengths and 4.5 bits of information.
evidence: Direct statement based on signal detection theory calculations.

claim: Time-window averaging smooths out fluctuations due to plasticity and other sources of variability including differences in the age of the synapses.
source: To explain the high precision observed in spine head volumes, we propose that time-window averaging smooths out fluctuations due to plasticity and other sources of variability including differences in the age of the synapses.
evidence: Direct statement proposing a mechanism.

claim: For release probability pr = 0.1 and presynaptic spiking rate R = 1 Hz, the averaging time window is 21.8 minutes.
source: Table 1 gives averaging time windows T = n/R, where R is spiking rate of the presynaptic axon, for representative values of pr and a range of spiking rates.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Table 1 showing the calculated values.

claim: For release probability pr = 0.1 and presynaptic spiking rate R = 25 Hz, the averaging time window is 52.2 seconds.
source: Table 1 gives averaging time windows T = n/R, where R is spiking rate of the presynaptic axon, for representative values of pr and a range of spiking rates.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Table 1 showing the calculated values.

claim: For release probability pr = 0.5 and presynaptic spiking rate R = 1 Hz, the averaging time window is 2.42 minutes.
source: Table 1 gives averaging time windows T = n/R, where R is spiking rate of the presynaptic axon, for representative values of pr and a range of spiking rates.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Table 1 showing the calculated values.

claim: For release probability pr = 0.5 and presynaptic spiking rate R = 25 Hz, the averaging time window is 5.8 seconds.
source: Table 1 gives averaging time windows T = n/R, where R is spiking rate of the presynaptic axon, for representative values of pr and a range of spiking rates.
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Table 1 showing the calculated values.

claim: Previous upper bounds on the variability of spine volume in the hippocampus underestimated the precision by including the spine neck volume.
source: Previous upper bounds on the variability of spine volume in the hippocampus, based on the whole spine volume (Sorra and Harris, 1993; O'Connor et al., 2005), underestimated the precision by including the spine neck volume (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), which was not correlated between pairs of spines in our volume (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Direct statement with citations and references to supplementary figures.

claim: The dense reconstruction included a complete inventory of every synapse in the reconstructed volume and was unbiased in this respect.
source: Our dense reconstruction included a complete inventory of every synapse in the reconstructed volume and in this respect was unbiased.
evidence: Direct statement about the completeness of the reconstruction.

claim: If 17 random pairs were chosen from all 287 synapses, there is only a one in 5000 chance that the spine heads would be as precisely matched as the 17 axon-coupled pairs discovered.
source: To make this p value concrete, if 17 random pairs were chosen from all 287 synapses in the reconstructed volume, there is only a one in 5000 chance that the spine heads would be as precisely matched as the 17 axon-coupled pairs discovered here.
evidence: Direct statement interpreting the statistical significance.

claim: Previous studies have shown that there is a high correlation of the size of the spine head with the PSD area and numbers of docked vesicles.
source: Previous studies have shown that there is a high correlation of the size of the spine head with the PSD area and numbers of docked vesicles (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Lisman and Harris, 1994; Harris and Sultan, 1995; Schikorski and Stevens, 1997; Murthy et al., 2001; Branco et al., 2008; Bourne et al., 2013).
evidence: Direct statement with multiple citations to supporting literature.

claim: The spine neck diameters were highly correlated between axon-coupled pairs of spines (r² = 0.70).
source: However, it was unexpected to find that the spine neck diameters were also highly correlated between axon-coupled pairs of spines (Figure 4D r2=0.70), since the correlation between spine head volumes and spine neck diameters is not statistically significant (Figure 1D).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: The correlation between spine head volumes and spine neck diameters is not statistically significant.
source: However, it was unexpected to find that the spine neck diameters were also highly correlated between axon-coupled pairs of spines (Figure 4D r2=0.70), since the correlation between spine head volumes and spine neck diameters is not statistically significant (Figure 1D).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: There are at least two geometric aspects of the spine geometry that are under tight control of synaptic plasticity.
source: Thus, there are at least two geometric aspects of the spine geometry that are under tight control of synaptic plasticity, which may reflect different aspects of synaptic function.
evidence: Inference drawn from the correlation data on spine head and neck diameter.

claim: The diameter of the spine neck may reflect the need for trafficking of materials between the spine shaft and spine head, which is known to be regulated by LTP and LTD.
source: The diameter of the spine neck may reflect the need for trafficking of materials between the spine shaft and spine head, which is known to be regulated by LTP and LTD (Araki et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative statement with citation to supporting work.

claim: Highly correlated release probability at multiple contacts in the neocortex between the axon of a given layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron and the same target cell has been reported.
source: Complementing our observations and analysis in the hippocampus, highly correlated pr at multiple contacts in the neocortex between the axon of a given layer 2/3 pyramidal neuron and the same target cell has been reported (Koester and Johnston, 2005).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to supporting work.

claim: In a recent connectomic reconstruction of the mouse cortex, the similarity in the volumes of axon-coupled pairs of dendritic spines were statistically significant.
source: In a recent connectomic reconstruction of the mouse cortex, the similarity in the volumes of axon-coupled pairs of dendritic spines were statistically significant (Kasthuri et al., 2015).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to supporting work.

claim: The same high precision of synaptic plasticity may be true in other brain areas.
source: This observation is further evidence for the high precision of synaptic plasticity and suggests that the same may be true in other brain areas.
evidence: Inference drawn from observations in mouse cortex.

claim: Synaptic tagging and capture is much less effective when the synapses are on different branches.
source: Synaptic tagging and capture, in which inputs that are too weak to trigger LTP or LTD can be 'rescued' by a stronger input to neighboring synapses if it occurs within an hour (Frey and Morris, 1997; O'Donnell and Sejnowski, 2014), is much less effective when the synapses are on different branches (Govindarajan et al., 2011), which would tend to make two synapses from the same axon on different dendritic branches less similar.
evidence: Direct statement with citations to supporting work.

claim: An unusual triple synapse from a single axon was excluded from the analysis because the presynaptic terminal was a single large varicosity filled with vesicles shared by three synapses.
source: An unusual triple synapse from a single axon (Figure 4B, 'k, l, m') was excluded from the analysis because the presynaptic terminal was a single large varicosity filled with vesicles (i.e. an MSB) shared by three synapses, unlike the other pairs that had isolated presynaptic specializations (n=9), or an MSB shared by two synapses (n=8).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: The estimate of variability would not be greatly affected by including the 3 additional pairs of synapses from the triple synapse in the analysis.
source: Regardless of the explanation, our estimate of the variability would not be greatly affected by including these 3 additional pairs of synapses in the analysis.
evidence: Direct statement about the robustness of the estimate.

claim: Phosphorylation of CaMKII integrates calcium signals over minutes to hours and is a critical step in enzyme cascades leading to structural changes induced by LTP and LTD.
source: Phosphorylation of calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII), required for spike-timing dependent plasticity processes, integrates calcium signals over minutes to hours and is a critical step in enzyme cascades leading to structural changes induced by long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD) (Kennedy et al., 2005), including rearrangements of the cytoskeleton (Kramár et al., 2012).
evidence: Direct statement with citations to supporting work.

claim: The time window over which CaMKII integrates calcium signals is within the range of time windows predicted to be needed to achieve the observed precision.
source: The time window over which CaMKII integrates calcium signals is within the range of time windows we predict would be needed to achieve the observed precision (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement comparing CaMKII time windows to predicted values in Table 1.

claim: Similar time windows occur in synaptic tagging and capture, which also requires CaMKII.
source: Similar time windows occur in synaptic tagging and capture, which also requires CaMKII (Redondo and Morris, 2011; de Carvalho Myskiw et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement with citations to supporting work.

claim: Biochemical pathways within the postsynaptic spine have the long time scales required to record and maintain the history of activity patterns leading to structural changes in the size of the spine heads.
source: These observations suggest that biochemical pathways within the postsynaptic spine have the long time scales required to record and maintain the history of activity patterns leading to structural changes in the size of the spine heads.
evidence: Inference drawn from observations about CaMKII and synaptic tagging.

claim: The information stored at a single synapse is encoded in the form of the synaptic strength, which reflects the pre- and postsynaptic history experienced by the synapse.
source: The information stored at a single synapse is encoded in the form of the synaptic strength, which reflects the pre- and postsynaptic history experienced by the synapse.
evidence: Direct statement about information encoding.

claim: Due to the many sources of variability, the information stored at a synapse cannot be read out with a single input spike.
source: But due to the many sources of variability, this information cannot be read out with a single input spike.
evidence: Direct statement about the limitation of single-spike readout.

claim: The stochastic variability might reflect a sampling strategy designed for energetic efficiency since it is the physical substrate that must be stable for long-term memory retention, not the read out of individual spikes.
source: First, the stochastic variability might reflect a sampling strategy designed for energetic efficiency since it is the physical substrate that must be stable for long-term memory retention, not the read out of individual spikes (Laughlin and Sejnowski, 2003).
evidence: Speculative statement with citation to supporting work.

claim: Each synapse in essence samples from a probability distribution with a highly accurate mean, which collectively produces a sample from the joint probability distribution across all synapses.
source: Each synapse in essence samples from a probability distribution with a highly accurate mean, which collectively produces a sample from the joint probability distribution across all synapses.
evidence: Speculative statement about the computational role of stochastic sampling.

claim: Drop out regularizes learning by reducing co-adaptation and overfitting.
source: Drop out regularizes the learning since a different network is being used on every learning trial, which reduces co-adaptation and overfitting.
evidence: Direct statement about the computational advantage of drop out.

claim: The upper bound on the variability may be limited by errors in the reconstruction and could be even lower with more accurate methods.
source: The upper bound on the variability that we have found may be limited by errors in the reconstruction and could be even lower if a more accurate method could be devised to compute the volume of a spine head, neck diameter, PSD area, number of docked vesicles, or other salient features of dendritic spines.
evidence: Direct statement about potential limitations and future improvements.

claim: There is a minimum of 26 distinguishable synaptic strengths.
source: We found that there is a minimum of 26 distinguishable synaptic strengths, corresponding to storing 4.7 bits of information at each synapse.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract.

claim: Because of stochastic variability of synaptic activation, the observed precision requires averaging activity over several minutes.
source: Because of stochastic variability of synaptic activation the observed precision requires averaging activity over several minutes.
evidence: Direct statement in the abstract.

claim: Synapses in the hippocampus are involved in the formation of new declarative memories.
source: Synapses in the hippocampus are involved in the formation of new declarative memories.
evidence: Direct statement based on established knowledge.

claim: The failure rate at synapses depends inversely on the strength, and therefore the size, of the synapse.
source: The failure rate at synapses depends inversely on the strength, and therefore the size, of the synapse.
evidence: Direct statement based on established knowledge.

claim: The strengths of weaker, smaller, and less reliable synapses would be expected to be less precisely controlled than larger and stronger synapses.
source: On this basis the strengths of weaker, and therefore smaller and less reliable synapses, would be expected to be less precisely controlled than the larger and stronger synapses, which have a lower failure rate.
evidence: Inference based on the relationship between failure rate and synapse size.

claim: The distributions of spine head volume, PSD area, docked vesicles, spine neck volume, spine neck diameter, and spine neck length are highly skewed with a long tail.
source: The strong correlations between these metrics, the skewed shape of the frequency histograms, and the number of synapses per unit of volume (Figures 1–3), are consistent with previous observations (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Schikorski and Stevens, 1997; Sorra et al., 2006; Bourne and Harris, 2011; Bourne et al., 2013; Bell et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figures 1-3 and citations to previous work.

claim: The number of synapses per unit of volume is consistent with previous observations.
source: The strong correlations between these metrics, the skewed shape of the frequency histograms, and the number of synapses per unit of volume (Figures 1–3), are consistent with previous observations (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Schikorski and Stevens, 1997; Sorra et al., 2006; Bourne and Harris, 2011; Bourne et al., 2013; Bell et al., 2014).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to figures and citations to previous work.

claim: The accuracy of measurements matched the precision of the spine.
source: The correlation between spine head area and spine head volume accounted for 99% of the variance, despite the wide range in spine head shapes and dimensions (Figure 1A), which suggests that the accuracy of our measurements matched the precision of the spine.
evidence: Inference drawn from the high correlation between measurements.

claim: Accurately maintaining the size of every synapse, regardless of size and strength, could be important for the function, flexibility and computational power of the hippocampus.
